procedural_history.impugned_order: The Labour Appellate Tribunal affirmed the award of the Industrial Tribunal, which held the company bound by its offer and awarded Rs. 45,000 to the workmen as their share of the profits.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Labour Appellate Tribunal of India, Third Bench, Lucknow, affirmed the award of the Industrial Tribunal in Appeal No. Calcutta 44 of 1952 on July 21, 1953.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant company (likely the company that owned the mills) approached the Supreme Court challenging the Labour Appellate Tribunal's judgment and decree, arguing that the initial notification was ultra vires, the reference and award were void, and there was no concluded agreement between the parties.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Government is competent to refer an industrial dispute for adjudication after the industry in question has been closed down, if the dispute arose prior to the closure.

facts: A dispute arose between the management and the workmen regarding a claim for a share of profits from the sale of the company's mills.
This claim and the resulting dispute originated on January 3 and January 10, 1951, while the industry was still in operation.
The industry was subsequently closed down on March 21, 1951.
After the closure, on November 16, 1951, the U.P. Government issued a notification to refer the pre-existing dispute for adjudication by an Industrial Tribunal.
law: Under Section 3 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, the government is empowered to refer an "industrial dispute" for adjudication.
An "industrial dispute," as defined in the Industrial Disputes Act, is a dispute that arises between employers and employees in connection with employment or conditions of labor.
The court affirmed the principle that an industrial dispute, to be valid, must arise out of an existing industry.
application: The appellant (the employer) argued that the government's reference was incompetent because, at the time of the notification, the industry had already closed and the employer-employee relationship no longer existed.
The Court rejected this argument, finding nothing in the language of Section 3 of the Act that required the industry to be in existence on the date of the government's reference.
The Court's reasoning was that the key condition for a valid reference is the existence of an "industrial dispute." An industrial dispute comes into being when it arises out of an existing industry.
In this case, the dispute over the share of profits arose in January 1951, when the industry was fully operational. Therefore, a valid industrial dispute existed at that time.

The Court held that once this condition is met (i.e., a dispute arises in an existing industry), the government's power to make a reference is complete. The subsequent closure of the industry does not nullify this power.

The Court reasoned that any other interpretation would lead to "serious anomalies and grave injustice," as it would allow an employer to commit unfair labor practices and then escape accountability simply by closing the business before the government could act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the government is competent to refer an industrial dispute for adjudication even after the industry has closed, provided that the dispute itself arose prior to the closure. Therefore, the government's notification was valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether a concluded and enforceable agreement existed between the management and the workmen for the payment of 25% of the profits from the sale transaction.

facts: The management offered to pay the workmen 25% of the profits from the sale of its machinery in a letter dated January 3, 1951.
This offer was expressly conditional on the workmen withdrawing their strike notice "at once and today."
The workmen did not accept this condition. Instead, their union made counter-proposals in a letter dated January 5, 1951.
On January 10, 1951, the management renewed its offer, again subject to the condition that the strike notice be withdrawn at once.
The union replied that the strike was not happening on the 12th but that they were waiting for a "final decision" from their leader, indicating no acceptance had occurred.
Subsequently, the workmen refused to cooperate with the management in dismantling the machinery, which was a key objective of the management's offer.
The workmen then entered into a direct contract with the purchaser to dismantle the machinery, causing the management to lose a contract worth at least Rs. 2 lakhs in profit.
law: For a concluded and enforceable agreement to exist, there must be a clear offer and an unconditional acceptance of that offer.
If an offer is made subject to a specific condition, that condition must be fulfilled for the acceptance to be valid.
A counter-proposal acts as a rejection of the original offer.
The question of whether there was consideration for a promise only arises after it is established that a concluded agreement was formed through offer and acceptance.
application: The Supreme Court examined the correspondence between the parties and found that the management's offer was never accepted.
The Court noted that the offer was explicitly conditional on the immediate withdrawal of the strike notice, a condition the workmen never fulfilled.
The union's response, which included counter-proposals and a statement that they were awaiting a final decision, was deemed a rejection of the offer, not an acceptance.

The Court rejected the argument that the workmen accepted the offer by their conduct (i.e., by not actually going on strike). It held that their subsequent actions, such as refusing to help dismantle the machinery and taking the dismantling contract for themselves, were entirely inconsistent with an acceptance of the management's proposal.

The Court found that the lower Tribunal had made a mistake by considering whether there was "consideration" for the promise. The Court clarified that since the offer was never accepted, no agreement was ever concluded, and therefore the question of consideration was irrelevant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no concluded and enforceable agreement between the management and the workmen. The workmen never accepted the management's conditional offer, and their subsequent actions demonstrated their opposition to the management's plan. Therefore, the claim for 25% of the sale profits was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Government is competent to refer an industrial dispute for adjudication after the industry in question has been closed down, if the dispute arose prior to the closure.
appellant_arguments: The notification referring the dispute to the Industrial Tribunal is ultra vires and void because it was issued after the business had been closed.
The right to the profit share, which is the subject of the dispute, accrued to the workmen only after the closure of the business, making the reference incompetent.
respondent_arguments: The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is determined by the date on which the right in dispute arises, not the date of the reference.
The machinery of the Act is available to resolve disputes over rights that accrued prior to the closure of the business.
The claim for a share of profits arose on January 3 and 10, 1951, when the industry was still working, making the reference valid even though the business closed on March 21, 1951.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a concluded and enforceable agreement existed between the management and the workmen for the payment of 25% of the profits from the sale transaction.
appellant_arguments: There was no concluded or binding agreement to pay the workmen any share of the profits from the sale.
The management's offers were conditional on the withdrawal of a strike notice, a condition that was never met by the workmen, causing the offers to lapse.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not disturb the Tribunal's finding of fact that a concluded and enforceable agreement existed.
The fact that the workmen did not go on strike and continued to work served as consideration for the management's promise, making it a binding agreement and a term of service.

statutes.act_name: Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act No. XLVIII of 1950

cases.principle: The Act has no retrospective operation.

cases.case_name: Messrs Burn and Go., Ltd., Calcutta v. Their Workmen
cases.citation: (1) Civil Appeal No. 325 of 1055, decided on October 11, 1956
cases.principle: The object of all labour legislation was firstly to ensure fair terms to the workmen, and secondly to prevent disputes between employers and employees, so that production might not be adversely affected and the larger interests of the public might not suffer.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An industrial dispute can be validly referred to a tribunal even after the closure of a business, provided the right that is the subject matter of the dispute arose prior to the closure. Discharge of workmen due to the closure of a business is distinct from discharge on retrenchment, as retrenchment implies the continuance of the industry and the discharge of only surplus labor.
obiter: The object of all labour legislation is to ensure fair terms to workmen and prevent disputes between employers and employees so that production might not be adversely affected, and these objects can have their fulfillment only in an existing and not a dead industry.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's competence to adjudicate an industrial dispute is determined by the date the dispute arose, not the date of the government's reference; a reference is valid if the dispute originated while the industry was operational, even if it later closed. However, the court found there was no concluded and enforceable agreement for profit sharing in this case, overturning the Tribunal's finding of fact because the Tribunal had "spoken in two voices, and has given inconsistent" findings, and therefore set aside the award of compensation.
legal_tests_applied: The power of the State to make a reference under section 3 must be determined with reference not to the date on which it is made but to the date on which the right which is the subject-matter of the dispute arises.
A distinction exists between the accrual of a right and the date it becomes payable; a right can be acquired 'in praesenti' (at the present time) even if the payment is deferred to a future date.
why_appellant_lost: On the issue of government competence, the appellant lost because the court found nothing in the language of section 3 of the Act to warrant the imposition of the limitation that the industry must be in existence on the date of the reference.

The court held that if the condition that an industrial dispute arose out of an existing industry is satisfied, the competence of the State for taking action is complete, and the fact that the industry has since been closed can have no effect on it.

The court rejected the appellant's factual argument that the right to profit share accrued after closure, reasoning that the workmen acquired a right 'in praesenti' to the profits when the promise was made, even though the amount was only payable at a later date.
why_respondent_won: On the issue of government competence, the respondent won because the court agreed that the State's power to make a reference is determined by the date the right in dispute arises, not the date of the reference itself.
The court affirmed that the machinery provided under the Act would be available for working out the rights which had accrued prior to the dissolution of the business.

The court found that the claim for a share of profits arose on January 3 and 10, 1951, when the industry was still working, which was sufficient to validate the reference made after the business had closed.
policy_considerations: Construing the Act to require an industry's continued existence at the time of reference would result in 'serious anomalies and grave injustice,' as a workman's statutory rights could be defeated by the timing of a closure.

Allowing a subsequent closure to invalidate a pre-existing dispute would create a loophole for an employer to indulge in unfair labour practices, victimisation, and wrongful dismissals and then escape the consequences by closing down the industry.
